source.title: Scaling Laws for Upcycling Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
source.authors: Seng Pei Liew; Takuya Kato; Sho Takase

record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out loss scaling in upcycled MoE models and refines a simple power-law account by finding an interaction between the dense-model and upcycled-training token budgets.
record.gate_note: The study reports loss-scaling fits, fit errors, and a derived compute-optimal upcycling relation. Its benchmark scores do not measure downstream predictability from scale or pretraining loss, so they are not rows for V6. It also reports that a data-splitting ablation has very small performance differences, but does not fit or test a scaling law for repeated data; this is not a V5 row. The learning-rate and auxiliary-loss ablations concern training setup rather than the scaling claims. Results cited from other studies are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study fits held-out cross-entropy scaling laws in a new regime: dense checkpoints upcycled to MoE. It covers tokens, active parameters, sparsity and dense size, validates the fits on held-out runs, and derives a compute-optimal allocation. It also fits Chinchilla-form laws for dense and from-scratch MoE baselines (Table 2). The results show the power-law form holds in this regime but needs a D1×D2 interaction term.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that upcycled MoE loss follows power-law scaling in dataset sizes and model configuration, with a novel dense×upcycled token interaction that reduces upcycling's efficiency at large budgets. The joint law extrapolates reliably for a fixed architecture. Upcycling beats from-scratch only for low sunk cost and token budget, and is compute-inefficient relative to from-scratch training when no pretrained model exists.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses dense-checkpoint upcycling into MoE models, fitting cross-entropy loss across dense and upcycled token budgets and MoE configurations. It uses WSD schedules and studies an interaction term; it is not a direct replication of the original dense-model scaling experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted dataset exponents vary with MoE architecture and dense-token budget D1; the fitted functional form affects fit quality. The reported Japanese and code datasets also differ in loss level and saturation behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: Upcycling beats from-scratch MoE only below a token threshold D* that shrinks with dense size (about 4B tokens for 8x1B). With no pretrained model, compute-optimal dense or MoE training beats upcycling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The efficiency of upcycling relative to from-scratch training diminishes with sunk cost and model size.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: The study says computational constraints limited the number of model-configuration data points and range. The joint-law extrapolation is summarized by a validation RMS of 0.015 without specifying an orders-of-magnitude extrapolation range. The main text and Appendix D.1 differ in which model-configuration functional form they identify as the best fit. Some additional-dataset scaling results are only shown in figures.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying scaling-law rows were omitted. Benchmark comparisons in Table 7 were left out because they do not test downstream predictability from scale or pretraining loss. The dataset-splitting/repetition ablation in Figure 10 reports a small performance difference but does not test a scaling law under repeated data.

untested.parts: Only small dense and MoE from-scratch fits (15M–1B dense) in Table 2. No multi-order-of-magnitude dense sweep and no compute scaling with other factors non-bottlenecked.
Prediction of runs orders of magnitude larger than the fitted ones; the extrapolation distance is not stated.
Dense compute-optimal allocation and the Kaplan vs Hoffmann split; only upcycling with fixed sunk cost is derived.
Depth, width or other shape at fixed parameter count; not studied.
Image or video modalities, fine-tuning or transfer laws, and repeated-data scaling laws; the repetition ablation fits no law.
Downstream predictability from scale or loss; benchmarks are reported only as a sanity check.
Parameter-counting conventions and their effect on published disagreements are not tested.

missing.what: Fitted Chinchilla-form parameters for dense and from-scratch MoE (A, B, α, β, shared E=0.165)
D2 power-law fits whose exponent decreases logarithmically with D1
Power-law loss in dense size N1 for the upcycled model
Alternative joint form rejected for yielding negative exponents; a unified law across regimes fits poorly
WSD vs cosine schedule give similar losses for dense and MoE

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V7 limits_scope label on R9 rests on a misread: main text and appendix agree on the additive form without interaction. The reader's V2 limits_scope on extrapolation magnitude concerns an untested part, not a qualification, so it is moved to untested. Rows were moved from V1 to V5 because upcycling is a two-stage regime. The study is not one of the original sources.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests text cross-entropy scaling in upcycled MoE models, not the general claim for dense language models or compute scaling with the other quantities non-bottlenecked.
The study reports validation RMS for its extrapolation, but does not establish prediction across runs orders of magnitude larger.

The compute allocation is derived for upcycling with a pretrained dense model and fixed sunk-cost condition; the study does not test the general dense-training allocation claims or compare Kaplan's and Hoffmann's allocation laws.
The study varies sparsity and active parameters, but does not test depth, width, or other architecture details at a fixed parameter count.

The study tests upcycling and scaling on Japanese-language and code datasets. It does not test image/video modalities, fine-tuning or transfer scaling, or a scaling law specifically under repeated data.
Benchmark performance is compared, but its predictability from model scale or pretraining loss is not tested.

The study examines dependence on dense-token budget, MoE architecture, dataset, and fitted functional form; it does not systematically test parameter-count conventions or training-schedule choices as causes of published scaling-law disagreements.

rows.note: The authors say loss improves with increased sparsity and active parameters within the tested range. Appendix D.1 gives competing fit errors and says the additive form without interaction has the best error, so the preferred fit description is not fully consistent across the text.

rows.subject: Upcycled MoE models

rows.operation_detail: Fit the joint held-out cross-entropy scaling law over dense tokens D1, upcycled tokens D2, and dense model size N1.

conditions.value: E fixed using a joint fit of dense and from-scratch MoE laws

rows.measure: Joint scaling-law form and validation RMS error
rows.value: L(D1,D2,N1)=A D1^-α1 D2^(-α2+α3 log D1)+B N1^-β2+E; validation RMS error 0.015
rows.note: The authors describe the fitted law as extrapolating well, but do not quantify the extrapolation distance or say it spans orders of magnitude.
rows.check: Remove V1 and V7; this is an upcycled joint law. The extrapolation range behind the 0.015 validation RMS is not stated.

source_check.correct: V5: observed conditional power-law scaling. V2: cannot_determine; validation RMS error is 0.015, but the text does not establish prediction across orders of magnitude.
source_check.problem: The observed state is justified for V5 but does not establish V2's required extrapolation distance.

rows.subject: Upcycled MoE models
rows.operation_detail: Derived compute-optimal token and model-size scaling for a fixed upcycled-training compute budget C2, with D1 fixed.
rows.measure: Compute-optimal scaling of D2 and N1 with C2
rows.value: D2opt ∝ C2^(β/(β+αeff)); N1opt ∝ C2^(αeff/(β+αeff)); αeff:=α2−α3 log D1
rows.note: This is an optimization derived from the fitted scaling law, not a direct empirical sweep of compute-optimal allocations.
rows.check: Analytic derivation from the fitted upcycling law, not an empirical sweep. The allocation exponent depends on D1 through αeff, so it is not a single stable power.

source_check.correct: V3: observed in the analytical allocation derived from the fitted law, with D1 fixed. Both allocation exponents are constant with respect to C2; no direct empirical optimum sweep is reported.
source_check.problem: Dependence of exponents on D1 does not make the fixed-D1 power laws partial.

rows.subject: Upcycled MoE models
rows.operation_detail: Applied the compute-optimal upcycling relation to cited Llama2 models.
rows.measure: Estimated relation between compute-optimal upcycling tokens and model size
rows.note: The paper says larger pretrained models require nearly quadratic increases in upcycling data.
rows.check: Not an empirical result. It projects the fitted law onto cited Llama2 sizes and token counts. The value D2 ∝ N1^1.8 does appear in Section 5.2, despite numbers_found 0/1.
